metaDescription: A smart home that starts at £5.49. Energy-monitoring smart plugs, Philips Hue, a 2K doorbell and a robot vacuum — compared on real UK prices, with the honest limits of each.
h1: The smart home that starts at £5.49 — and tells you what it is costing you
intro: Most smart home shopping goes wrong in the same way: people buy a hub, a bundle and a set of bulbs before they have any idea what they will actually use. Here is the other way in — start with one plug that measures your electricity, find out which appliance is quietly costing you the most, and build from there. Everything on this page is in stock at Megastore76 right now, at the price shown.

products.summary: This is the cheapest thing on the page and, for most people, the most useful. A smart plug on its own is a novelty — you can turn a lamp on from your phone, which you could already do by walking over and pressing the switch. The difference here is the energy monitoring. Plug it into the appliance you suspect, leave it a day, and the app tells you what that appliance actually draws. Most people find the culprit is not the thing they expected.

guide.heading: Six things worth knowing before you spend anything
guide.intro: None of this is complicated, but getting the order wrong is how people end up with £300 of kit they never use.

points.h: Energy monitoring is the only feature that pays you back
points.p: Voice control is convenient. Scheduling is convenient. Neither saves you money. A plug that reports power draw is the one smart home feature that can actually change a bill, because it tells you which appliance is the expensive one — and it is usually not the one people assume. That is why the £5.49 plug is the pick at the top of this page rather than something more impressive.

points.h: You almost certainly do not need a hub to start
points.p: Wi-Fi smart plugs connect straight to your router, so you can begin with one plug and no hub at all. The exception is Hue, which uses the Zigbee radio standard and needs the Bridge — but the Bridge comes in the starter kit, so you are not buying it separately.

points.h: Wi-Fi, Zigbee and Matter are not the same thing
points.p: Wi-Fi devices connect directly but each one takes a slot on your network. Zigbee devices, like Hue, talk to a hub instead, which keeps your Wi-Fi cleaner once you have a lot of them. Matter is the newer cross-brand standard meant to make everything work together — support is improving, but it is still worth checking the specific device you are buying rather than assuming.

points.h: Voice assistant lock-in is real, so pick deliberately
points.p: Most plugs on this page work with both Alexa and Google, which is the safest position. The Echo Dot is obviously Alexa-first. If you already have a house full of one assistant, buy for that one rather than starting a second ecosystem by accident.

points.h: Buy one, live with it, then buy more
points.p: The most common expensive mistake is buying a bundle of four or six devices before knowing how you will use them. One plug, one week, and you will know whether you want four more or whether you have answered your question and can stop. The 4-pack is better value per plug — but only if you were going to buy four anyway.

points.h: What smart home kit genuinely cannot do
points.p: A smart plug switches power. It cannot dim a lamp, control anything with a physical dial, or run a boiler. None of these devices will fix poor Wi-Fi — a doorbell with a weak signal at the front of the house will give you poor footage no matter how good the camera is. And a robot vacuum at this price maintains a floor; it does not replace cleaning it properly.

faqHeading: Common questions about smart home gear

faq.q: What is the cheapest way to start a smart home?
faq.a: One Wi-Fi smart plug. At £5.49 the Tuya plug needs no hub, connects straight to your router, works with Alexa, and includes energy monitoring. You will know within a week whether smart home is something you actually want before you spend anything more.

faq.q: Do I need a hub for any of these?
faq.a: Only for Philips Hue. The Hue bulbs use Zigbee rather than Wi-Fi, so they need the Bridge — which is included in the starter kit, so it is not a separate purchase. Every smart plug and the doorbell here connect directly to your Wi-Fi.

It is accurate enough to be useful, which is the point. The reading tells you what a device is drawing in real time, so you can compare one appliance against another and find the expensive one. Treat it as a tool for comparison rather than as a substitute for your electricity meter.

faq.q: Will these work with the Alexa or Google device I already own?
faq.a: The smart plugs work with both Alexa and Google Home, so either assistant is fine. Philips Hue supports Alexa, Google and Apple HomeKit. The Echo Dot is Amazon's own, so it is Alexa by design.

faq.q: Is Philips Hue worth it compared to cheap colour bulbs?
faq.a: If you want one lamp to change colour, no — cheap Wi-Fi colour bulbs cost far less and will do that. Hue is worth the money if you want a lighting system: reliable Zigbee connection that does not load your Wi-Fi, colour that matches across bulbs, and the ability to grow room by room without replacing anything.

faq.q: Can a smart plug control anything in my house?
faq.a: No, and this trips people up. A smart plug switches power to whatever is plugged into it, so it suits lamps, heaters, fans and chargers. It cannot dim a light, control an appliance with a mechanical dial, or operate anything that needs to stay on — a freezer on a smart plug is a bad idea.

faq.q: Which robot vacuum should I buy?
faq.a: The one on this page is a compact, app-controlled model at £149.99 aimed at daily maintenance — dust, pet hair and crumbs — rather than deep cleaning. If you want mapping, no-go zones and far stronger suction, expect to pay considerably more; the cheaper robots in the store use simpler navigation.

faq.q: Why do some products on this page have no picture?
faq.a: Because their listing pictures failed a check we run on every image here. We look at each one for a claim the store cannot support — a price that contradicts the checkout, or a rating, award or review count, when the store has no customer reviews at all — and for a picture that shows a different product from the one named on the listing. Four failed: the WiFi Smart Plug 4-Pack, whose image prints an Editors’ Pick award and a 9.2/10 score the store has never been given, and shows US 125-volt hardware on a UK product; the Tommee Tippee GroEgg2, whose picture implies a Wi-Fi connection the nightlight does not have; the Anker Soundcore Work, pictured with no Anker branding; and the Compact Robot Vacuum, pictured as another brand’s robot vacuum. All four are still compared and priced above — they just have no picture, because a wrong picture is worse than none. The same check ran over the rest of the department, which is why the £23.78 desk lamp, the £15.97 LED strip, the £74.68 OKP robot vacuum, the £85 Proscenic and the £59.99 UR1 are absent from the grid below as well: every one of those five graphics prints a price between £1 and £99 that the store does not charge. A product with no picture is a lost sale; a product with a picture that misstates the price is a refund and a complaint. That is the trade we made.
